sections.title: Direct and indirect objects
sections.content:
Some verbs can be followed by two objects. Usually the first object (= the indirect object (IO)) is a person or group of people and the second object (= the direct object (DO)) is a thing:
• Can you bring me (= IO) some milk (= DO) from the shops?
• He made himself (= IO) a cup of coffee. (= DO)
We can often reverse the order of the objects if we put for or to before the IO (this is then called a prepositional object). Compare:
• I built my daughter a doll’s house. and I built a doll’s house for my daughter.
• Can you pass me that bandage? and Can you pass that bandage to me?

sections.title: For vs To
sections.content:
Some verbs can be used with either for or to. Often there is a difference in meaning: to suggests that there is a transfer of something to someone, and for suggests that someone benefits from something. Compare:
• I hadn’t got time to visit Mira, so I wrote a letter to her. (transfer)
• Mira had broken her wrist, so I wrote a letter for her. (benefit)
Also: bring, leave, pay, play, post, read, sell, send, sing, take

sections.title: Verbs that don’t take two objects
sections.content:
Some verbs that are followed by two objects cannot have their objects reversed with for / to:
• We all envied him his lifestyle. (but not We all envied his lifestyle for / to him.)
Also: allow, ask, cost, deny, forgive, guarantee, permit, refuse

sections.title: Describe and Fix
sections.content:
Some verbs, such as describe and fix, can only have a second object if this is a prepositional object:
• She described the situation (to me). (not She described me the situation.)
• He fixed the tap (for me). (not He fixed me the tap.)
Also: admit, announce, demonstrate, explain, introduce, mention, point out, prove, report, say, suggest (with to)
Also: collect, mend, repair (with for)

exercises.question: Elias hasn't got any money so I'll have to pay the bill ___ him.
exercises.hint: 'Pay for someone' = cover the cost on their behalf.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: for
'Pay for someone' means to cover their cost: 'I'll pay for him'. Compare: 'pay someone' = hand money directly to them. 'Pay for + person/thing' is the correct pattern when meeting an expense on behalf of someone.

exercises.question: You're staying with Dimitra at the weekend. Can you take this present ___ her?
exercises.explanation:
Answer: to
'Take something to someone' = deliver or bring it to their location. 'Take something for someone' would mean take it on their behalf for a different purpose. Here, delivering the present → 'to'.

exercises.sentence: Could you describe me the symptoms you've been experiencing?
exercises.correction: Could you describe the symptoms you've been experiencing to me?
exercises.hint: 'Describe' takes 'describe X to Y' — not a double object.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: describe the symptoms to me
'Describe' does not take a double object. Like 'explain' and 'suggest', it requires: describe + direct object + to + person. You cannot say 'describe me something' — the indirect object always needs 'to'. Compare: 'tell me something' (tell takes double object) vs 'describe something to me'.

exercises.question: He described us the house. (Correct if necessary)
options: He described the house to us.
He described for us the house.
He described the house for us.
exercises.hint: Describe only takes a prepositional object with 'to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: He described the house to us.
Describe only takes a prepositional object with 'to'. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: She explained me the problem. (Correct if necessary)
options: She explained the problem to me.
She explained me about the problem.
She explained the problem for me.
exercises.hint: Explain only takes a prepositional object with 'to'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She explained the problem to me.
Explain only takes a prepositional object with 'to'. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.sentence: She recommended me a very good dentist near the office.
exercises.correction: She recommended a very good dentist to me.
acceptable: recommended a very good dentist to me
exercises.hint: 'Recommend' takes 'recommend X to Y' — not a double object.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She recommended a very good dentist to me
'Recommend' does not take a double object — use 'recommend + thing + to + person'. This is consistent with 'suggest', 'describe', 'explain', 'propose'. Contrast with 'give', 'send', 'offer', 'show', 'tell' — which all accept double objects.

exercises.question: I prepared them a meal. (Correct if necessary)
options: I prepared a meal for them.
I prepared them for a meal.
I prepared a meal to them.
exercises.hint: Prepare usually takes DO + for + IO.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I prepared a meal for them.
Prepare usually takes DO + for + IO. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: I'll have to send him an email to explain the problem ___ him.
exercises.hint: 'Explain something to someone' — 'explain' never takes a double object.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: to
'Explain' always uses 'to + person': 'explain the problem to him'. Unlike 'give', 'tell', or 'send', 'explain' never takes a double object. Wrong: 'explain him the problem'. Correct: 'explain the problem to him'.

exercises.question: He ___ her a beautiful bunch of flowers on their anniversary.
exercises.hint: 'Give' takes a double object: give + person + thing.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: gave
'Give' follows the double-object pattern: give + indirect object (person) + direct object (thing). This pattern is shared by: give, send, offer, lend, owe, show, tell, teach, pay, bring, take, hand, pass. The alternative: 'gave flowers to her' (prepositional object).

exercises.question: A: Your new motorbike must have cost ___.
exercises.hint: Cost is a verb that doesn't reverse objects with for/to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: you a fortune
Cost is a verb that doesn't reverse objects with for/to. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: I poured Ben a drink and gave the glass ___ him.
exercises.hint: 'Give X to Y' — prepositional pattern, not double object here.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: to
'Give the glass to him' uses the prepositional pattern. 'Give him the glass' uses the double-object pattern. Both are correct for 'give', but the sentence already has 'poured Ben a drink' (double object), so the parallel prepositional form 'gave the glass to him' is more natural here.
